Console Philosophy & Gear Opinions

Why I Don't Use DiGiCo Consoles — And What I Use Instead

By Ryan Goldbacher · September 20, 2026

What console does Ryan Goldbacher use?

Short answer: I'm not a DiGiCo fan. I've mixed on them, I know engineers who get great results on them, and they're reliable — they're just not my tool. I currently mix on Allen & Heath, and from what I've heard, the Yamaha DM7 and PM series are probably the best-sounding digital desks out there right now.

This isn't a brand war. It's about what lets me work the way I need to work.

My Console History in One Paragraph

I started on analog — PM5D was just coming out when I began touring, M7CL was the cheaper version. They were reliable, you could get a mix going, but they lacked sonically. The first digital consoles that actually sounded good were the Pro Series and Avid Venue (first ones you could run plugins on). I knew Pro Tools from studio work, so Avid made sense. But nowadays I'm Allen & Heath. I like the way they sound, I'm good at getting them sounding good, and that's what matters.

Why Not DiGiCo?

I made a video about this that went viral on Instagram and Facebook — not because I was trying to start something, but because I said what I actually think. The core of it:

  • Sound character: "A $150k price tag doesn't buy you a good sounding desk." To my ears, DiGiCo sounds clinical — what I call "hospital hallway" sound. Clean, sterile, no grit.
  • What I want: "I want a console that fights me back a little bit and have it punch me in the gut than have it be super clean." I want character, tension, something that pushes back.
  • Fader feel: Multiple engineers have commented the fader quality feels cheap. That matters when you're riding faders for two hours a night.

When DiGiCo's official Instagram account replied to my roast with "Much respect to you!" — I replied "I still have respect for all the DiGiBros." That's the point. People get great mixes on DiGiCo. It's just not my pair of shoes.

What I Use Instead: Allen & Heath

Right now I'm an Allen & Heath guy. Here's why:

  • Sound: I like the way they sound. The preamps have the "grit" I'm looking for — what one commenter called "the preamps might be 'clean', but the tension is filthy."
  • Workflow: I'm good at getting them sounding good. That's not marketing — that's 20+ years of turning knobs until it works.
  • Value: I have an Allen & Heath SQ rack mount that has more inputs than my PM5D did 20 years ago, and the PM5D was almost $100k when it came out.

What I'd Use If I Wasn't on Allen & Heath: Yamaha

I don't have a ton of seat time on the new Yamaha DM7 and PM series, but what I have used tells me: they're probably the best sounding desks out there. Yamaha's been refining digital console sound for decades — PM5D, M7CL, PM10, Rivage — each generation gets closer. If you want clinical precision that still has musicality, that's the direction.

The Philosophy: "It's Just a Pair of Shoes"

This is the hill I'll die on: Your console is a tool. Use the one that fits you.

"It's just a pair of shoes that you're comfortable with, you know? If you can figure out how to make it work for you, it doesn't matter what anybody else thinks."

I've seen engineers refuse gigs because the house console wasn't their preferred brand. That's the wrong mindset. If you're so married to a piece of gear that you can't work without it, you're not an engineer — you're a template runner.

People get killer mixes on X32s. People get killer mixes on DiGiCo. People get killer mixes on analog Heritage 3000s. The console doesn't make the mix. You do.

Digital Console Evolution: What Actually Changed

For context — I've lived through the entire digital console transition:

EraConsolesReality
Early 2000sPM5D, M7CLReliable, workflow OK, sonically lacking
Mid 2000sAvid Venue, Pro SeriesFirst good-sounding digital, plugin integration
2010sDiGiCo SD series, Yamaha Rivage, Midas ProEverything got usable; brand preference dominates
2020sDM7, Quantum, Avantis, SQRack mounts out-spec 2000s flagships at 1/10 the price

The gap between "pro" and "entry level" has collapsed. An SQ has more I/O than a PM5D. The engineering is there at every price point now. The difference is workflow, sound character, and ecosystem — not capability.

What This Means for You

If you're choosing a console — for a tour, an install, a venue — here's my framework:

  1. Can you get a mix on it? Yes? Good. Move on.
  2. Does the workflow match how you think? Some consoles fight you; some get out of your way.
  3. Does the sound character serve the music? Clean isn't always better. Grit isn't always better. Match the tool to the gig.
  4. Can you fix it when it breaks? Reliability, parts availability, local support — boring but critical.
  5. Stop reading reviews. Start turning knobs. You'll learn 10x more in one soundcheck than a year of forum debates.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is DiGiCo a bad console?
No. It's reliable, widely used, and plenty of top engineers choose it. It's just not my preference.

What's the best live sound console?
There isn't one. The best console is the one you know deeply enough to push to its limits. For me that's Allen & Heath. For you it might be DiGiCo, Yamaha, Midas, or Avid.

Do you hate digital consoles?
No. I started in studios on Pro Tools. I've mixed on every major digital platform. I just prefer consoles with character over clinical precision.

What console would you recommend for a small venue?
Whatever fits the budget and the operator. Allen & Heath SQ, Yamaha TF/CL, Midas M32, Behringer X32 — they'll all do the job if you know how to use them.
